docs.text: Backup and recovery One of the benefits of DEW is the ability to backup and recover a previous version seamlessly. Version history DEW automatically stores a version for every save performed for the experiment and allows you to revert to an earlier version. To know more about how to revert to a version, click here Google drive If the user is saving to google drive, previous versions can of the files can be viewed and you can revert to a particular version in google drive. However, to get the changes in google drive reflected in DEW, the user must reupload the DEW file .

docs.text: Basics This guide provides a quick introduction to Distributed Experiment Workflows (DEW). What is DEW? DEW is an attempt to encode behavior and toplogical constraints which help with realization on testbeds. DEW consists of 3 major components. They are Actors, Scenario/Behavior, Constraints, and Bindings. Actors Actors are the different types of machines where the experiment is run. Scenario/Behavior Scenario defines the behavior of the components of the experiment. They consist of the action(command or script being executed) and the actor(the machine or component executing the action). To ensure the order of execution of actions, we use events. An actor emits one or more events when an action is completed. We use the emit keyword for this. Similarly, an actor waits for one for more events to perform an action. The when keyword is used for this. Sometimes, we may have multiple instances of an actor and we need to define whether to wait for events from all instances or any instance. Hence, we add ALL or ANY keyword before the events. We may also sometimes need to wait for a certain amount of time before executing an action. For this purpose, the wait keyword is used. It accepts either a number or a variable which can be filled later. Hence, a statement in scenario will look like [when [ALL/ANY] <events>][wait <time>] actor action [emit <events>] (The parts enclosed in square brackets are optional.) Constraints Constraints define the constraints for a single or a group of actors. There are seven different types of constraints allowed. They are os OS helps us define the operating system of the actor. The format of the constraint is os actor os_name num num constraint defines the number of instances of an actor. The format of the constraint is num actor number_of_instances link link adds a link between two actors. If there are multiple number of instances, you need to define the keyword ALL or ANY to indicate whether all instances need to be linked or any instance needs to be linked. The format of the constraint is link [ALL/ANY] actor1 [ALL/ANY] actor2 lan Add a particular actor to a LAN network. lan actor lan_name Check this . interfaces Yet to add location Yet to add nodetype Yet to add Bindings Bindings provide a mapping for actions or events and the scripts or commands. In the DEW file, the key and value of mappings are separated by space. DEW file format The DEW file format consists of each section defined inside square brackets. The format is [Scenario] <scenario_statements> [Bindings] <bindings> [Constraints] <constraint_statements> Benefits Robust design - DEW helps the researcher to think about dependencies and ordering and having a more robust design History - DEW keeps a history of all changes in the experiment which helps in restoring to a particular version when things go wrong Sharing and reuse - Since experiments can be shared, multiple researchers can collaborate on a single experiment.

docs.text: Dashboard This is the main page shown after logging in. The dashboard provides a list of experiments and options to create a new experiment, edit an existing experiment or logout. Clicking on the menu bar (≡) shows your name, picture, and the logout button. Clicking on the close button removes the menu bar. Click on an experiment to open the experiment page. Each experiment contains the name, creation date, last updated date and the role you have in the experiment. The roles possible are - Admin - Have access to edit and manage access for the experiment. This is the default role assigned to the creator on creating a new experiment. Developer - Have access to edit experiment but is not allowed to manage users and roles for the experiment. Spectator - Have read only access to the experiment. You can filter the experiments by using the options in the left side of the page. Clicking on the create page allows you to create a new experiment. You will be redirected to the experiment page on create or clicking an experiment.
docs.title: Dashboard

docs.text: Experiment page This is the main page used to edit experiments. Experiment name The name of the experiment is displayed on the top left corner of the page. To edit the name, click on the name and update the text. (just like google docs) The name can be a maximum of 101 characters. The number of characters remaining is shown to the right of the name. Menu bar The menu bar is colored green when the experiment does not contain any unsaved changes. It is colored grey if the experiment contains unsaved changes. The status is also shown next to the access level to the right. The access you have with the experiment is shown in the rightmost column. The various buttons and their functions are as follows Back button Click on the back button to go to the dashboard. Alternatively, you can use the back button in the browser. File menu This menu contains a number of file related operations. They are - Save Clicking on save will save the current experiment to the database. Save to google drive This button allows you to save the experiment to google drive. The experiment is saved in DEW format. The user will have a top level directory called “Distributed Experiment Workflows”. Inside the top level directory, we have folders created for each experiment. Files related to the experiment will be contained in the experiment’s folder For example, if we have an experiment named "test", the dew file is located at MyDrive > Distributed Experiment Workflows > test > test.dew Delete Deletes the experiment. Version history View the changes done previously to the experiment. To revert to a particular version, click on the revert button Share to user Share the experiment to another DEW user for access List of users View and manage the list of users who can access the experiment Share link Share the experiment to the public by generating a unique link Close Close the experiment and go back to the dashboard Create When the experiment is not saved at all, you get a create button which saves the experiment. Input This menu allows the user to upload an experiment using different methods. Upload Upload DEW files to load the experiment. For example, the dew file saved in google drive can be used for upload. NLP Write using natural language to generate DEW statements. The idea is to just type in the requirements and the appropriate DEW file is generated. This feature is currently experimental and may not work as expected for all cases. Export This menu is used to export the experiment to different formats NS file Download the NS file for the current experiment BASH file Download the Bash scripts for running the given experiment Dependency graph In order to understand the experiment better, we have a graph view which displays the experiment as a flowchart. The graph viewer also supports editing edges. To access the graph, click on the Dependency graph option in the menu bar. To go back to the experiment, click on the Experiment option in the menu bar. Editing edges To add an edge, toggle the switch, click on the source (hold the button and do not release) and drag the arrow till the destination. To delete an edge, click on the red box next to the edge. Please note that the mouse icon changes when a node or edge is clickable. Zoom and scroll To zoom in or zoom out, use the (+) and (-) buttons to increase or decrease the zoom level Please use the panning functionality instead of scrolling. (Click on the white area and drag in the desired direction) Behavior, Constraints, and Bindings In DEW, an experiment consists of a scenario (who does what and when), constraints (how experiment should be materialized on a testbed) and bindings (specific commands to run on nodes for each action). Behavior Behavior defines the steps to be executed during this experiment. Behavior statements will be in the form of [when <event>][wait <time>] actor action [emit <event>] For example: actor0 start_log wait t0 actor1 legitimate when stop_attack_done wait t3 actor1 stop_legitimate emit stop_legitimate_done As you start typing there will be auto-suggestion displayed near the top of the text area. Press tab to use the first auto suggested word. It will append the word near the cursor in the textarea. There will also be suggestion displayed along with suggested text. This will help you to write the next word or phrase. Constraints The constraints section defines all the constraints for this experiment. The statements will be in the form of actor constraint_type value The allowed constraint types are os num link lan interfaces location nodetype For example: os server ubuntu num attacker 3 lan client attacker link router server As you start typing there will be auto-suggestion displayed near the top of the text area. Press tab to use the first auto suggested word. It will append the word near the cursor in the textarea. There will also be suggestion displayed along with suggested text. This will help you to write the next word or phrase. Bindings Define all the constraints for this experiment. Choose an option from drop-down boxes or input your own commands. Variables are preceded by $ to indicate that their values should be replaced by constants in the design stage, or specified by user at run-time on the command line. For example: install_iperf apt-get install iperf -y install_tcpdump apt-get install tcpdump -y install_flooder /scripts/common/install_flooder.sh start_server iperf -s As you start typing behavior above this area will be populated with the terms which require definition for the experiment to execute.

docs.text: Sharing and Collaboration One of the benefits of DEW is the ability to share and collaborate with multiple people. It is possible to share directly on the UI or to use Google drive. Sharing in DEW To share an experiment with another user, both users must have accounts in DEW. Along with sharing, the creator of the experiment can also control the access a user has for the experiment. Access levels There are 3 levels Spectator/Read only - The user can only view the experiment but cannot change it. Developer/Write - The user can change the contents of the experiment but cannot change sharing settings Admin/Manage - The user will have the ability to change all aspects of an experiment. The creator of the experiment will have this level of access. Sharing in Google Drive Another way to share with others is to save the experiment to google drive. After saving to google drive, the user can share the files to anyone just like any other folder or file on google drive. To know more about how to save to google drive, click here .
